## Chart 4: Column Chart of Continental Means

### Implementation (Comparison: One Variable across a Few Items)

Chart 4 completes the Abela comparison branch at its coarsest grain: one variable
(the Happy Planet Index) across a few items (the five continents). Continents are
ordered by mean HPI with `forcats::fct_reorder()` rather than alphabetically, so
the ranking is read from position along a common baseline (Cleveland & McGill
1984) instead of recovered by scanning labels. The mean here is **unweighted**,
which distinguishes it from the population-weighted mean in Chart 1; the two
figures are not interchangeable and the subtitle says so. Because a continental
mean conceals how many countries it averages — four for Oceania against seventeen
for Asia — the count is printed inside each column rather than relegated to a
footnote.

![Mean Happy Planet Index by continent, 2024. Columns ordered from highest to lowest mean; the white label inside each column gives the number of countries behind the mean.](images/chart4_continent_means.png){fig-alt="Column chart of mean Happy Planet Index by continent. The Americas lead, followed by Oceania, Europe, Asia and Africa, with country counts printed inside each column."}

### The code

The chart runs against `hpi_clean`, the cleaned 2024 subset shared by the whole
team, and the palette and `theme_hackathon()` come from `R/theme.R` so that all
four charts share one visual language.

```{r}
#| eval: false
df_chart4 <- hpi_clean %>%
  group_by(continent) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_hpi = mean(hpi, na.rm = TRUE),
    n        = dplyr::n(),
    .groups  = "drop"
  ) %>%
  mutate(continent_ordered = fct_reorder(continent, mean_hpi, .desc = TRUE))

p4 <- ggplot(df_chart4, aes(x = continent_ordered, y = mean_hpi, fill = continent)) +
  geom_col(
    width = 0.68,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = sprintf("%.1f", mean_hpi)),
    vjust = -0.55,
    size = 3.6,
    fontface = "bold",
    color = "#222222"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(y = 1.8, label = paste0("n = ", n)),
    size = 2.9,
    color = "#FFFFFF",
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  scale_fill_continent() +
  scale_x_discrete(name = "Continent") +
  scale_y_continuous(
    name   = "Mean Happy Planet Index Score (0-100 Scale)",
    limits = c(0, 62),
    breaks = seq(0, 60, by = 10),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    title    = "The Americas Convert Resources into Wellbeing More Efficiently Than Any Other Continent",
    subtitle = "Unweighted mean Happy Planet Index of the countries in each continent; n gives the number of countries behind each column.",
    caption  = "Source: Happy Planet Index (2024 Edition) | EPPS 6356 Hackathon"
  ) +
  theme_hackathon(legend_pos = "none") +
  theme(
    # theme_hackathon() re-declares axis.title.y through %+replace% without an
    # angle, which prints the title flat and squeezes the panel; the same fix
    # is applied in Chart 1.
    axis.title.y = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 2, margin = margin(r = 10))
  )

p4
```

Script: [`assignments/Chart4.R`](https://github.com/nedretsencavus/portfolio/blob/main/assignments/Chart4.R)

### Analytical Takeaway

- **The Americas lead on efficiency, not on income.** At a mean of **53.5** across
  sixteen countries, the Americas sit roughly four points above Oceania (**49.7**)
  and nearly six above Europe (**47.9**), despite a lower average GDP per capita
  than Europe. This is the HPI's central claim made visible at continental scale:
  the index rewards converting resources into long, satisfying lives, not
  accumulating resources.
- **Africa's position is a footprint artefact as much as a wellbeing one.**
  Africa's mean of **36.3** is the lowest of the five, but the cohort spreads from
  21.1 to 47.6 — a range wider than the gap between the top two continents.
  Reading the column as a statement about "Africa" rather than about its mean
  would be exactly the error the embedded counts are there to resist.
- **Oceania's column is the least reliable and says so.** Four countries stand
  behind a mean of **49.7**, against seventeen behind Asia's **43.3**. Printing
  `n` inside the bar keeps that asymmetry in the reader's eye at the moment of
  comparison; without it, five columns of identical construction imply five
  estimates of identical precision.
- **Sorting is the analysis.** Ordering by mean rather than alphabetically turns
  the ranking into a single left-to-right read. Wickham (2010) names alphabetical
  ordering of categorical variables as a common and avoidable fault, after
  Wainer's "Alabama first!"; here, sorting is what allows the title's claim to be
  verified by looking.

## What I had to fix

- **The y-axis title came out horizontal.** `theme_hackathon()` re-declares
  `axis.title.y` through `%+replace%` without an `angle`, so the angle resets to
  zero, the title prints flat at the far left, and the panel is squeezed. I caught
  it by comparing my first render against Chart 1, where the same fix
  (`element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 2, margin = margin(r = 10))`) already
  appears. Commit `07f074f`.
- **The first draft of the commit would have touched the whole repository.** The
  clone is on Windows, so every text file in the repo showed as modified on line
  endings alone — 13,521 insertions and 13,527 deletions across 52 files, all
  whitespace. I staged only the paths I had actually added instead of using
  `git add -A`, so the history stays readable.
- **`source("R/theme.R")` pointed at a file that was not in the repository.**
  `Chart1.R` and `Chart3.R` both call it, but the theme existed only inside the
  setup chunk of the Quarto document, so those two scripts failed from a clean R
  session.

## Beyond the chart

Extracting `R/theme.R` — the Okabe–Ito palette, the `scale_*` helpers and
`theme_hackathon()` — made every chart script runnable from a clean clone, which
closed the *"code runs from a clean R session using only the repo contents"* item
on the eligibility checklist for the whole team, not just for my chart.

I also wrote the team `README.md` (reproduction steps, package list, repo layout,
data source) and opened `prompts.md`, the shared AI disclosure, with my own
section filled in; and I generated `sessionInfo.txt`.
